PUT sets the resource to exactly the body, so a second identical PUT changes nothing more. GET is safe (and therefore idempotent). PATCH and POST are not idempotent in general: `{"op": "add", ...}` or 'append a comment' applied twice does twice the work.
explain_choice: Sending the same body again still asks the server to perform the action again, such as creating a second order.
A patch can be a relative change, such as incrementing a counter, so repeating it changes the result; the spec does not require PATCH to be idempotent.
GET is idempotent, but it is also safe, and the question asks for a method that changes state.

qs.q: A request through your load balancer returns 502. What does that tell you?
a: The proxy got an invalid response, or none, from the server behind it
The server behind the proxy was too slow, so the proxy gave up waiting
The service is overloaded or in maintenance and refusing work
Your request was malformed, and the server couldn't parse it
qs.e: 502 Bad Gateway is sent by an intermediary about its upstream: the backend crashed, closed the connection, or sent something that was not valid HTTP. The neighbouring codes separate the cases: 504 is the upstream timing out, 503 is 'unavailable right now', and 4xx codes blame the client. So a 502 sends you to the backend's logs, not your request.
explain_choice: An upstream that is too slow gives 504 Gateway Timeout.
Overload or maintenance is 503 Service Unavailable, often with Retry-After.
A malformed request is a client error, 400, not a 5xx.

qs.q: A client times out on `POST /payments` and retries with the same `Idempotency-Key` header. What must the server do for the retry to be safe?
a: Store the key with the first result and replay that result for repeats
Hash the request body and drop any body it has already processed before
Reject the repeat with 409 so the client knows it was a duplicate
Nothing extra: sending a key header makes the POST idempotent
qs.e: The client's timeout may have come after the payment was taken, so the retry must not charge again, and the client still needs to learn the result. The server records the key atomically with the result of the first request (the new payment's ID and status) and replays that response for the same key. Identical bodies are not duplicates in general: two genuine £10 payments look alike.
explain_choice: Two legitimate payments can have identical bodies; only a key the client chose per logical operation separates a retry from a new request.
A 409 leaves the client unsure whether its payment happened; replaying the original response tells it. 409 fits only a repeat that arrives while the first is still in progress.
The header is only a promise from the client; the server's stored key-to-result mapping is what makes the retry harmless.

qs.q: What does TCP guarantee to the application?
a: An ordered, reliable byte stream, with no message boundaries
Each send() call arrives as exactly one matching recv() on the other side
Delivery within a bounded time, or an error at once
Encryption of the bytes between the two endpoints
qs.e: TCP numbers every byte, retransmits what is lost and reorders what arrives early, so the receiver reads the same bytes in the same order. It says nothing about grouping: two sends can arrive in one recv, or one send across several. That is why every protocol on TCP needs framing, such as a length prefix or a delimiter. Latency is unbounded, and encryption is TLS's job.
explain_choice: TCP is a stream: sends can be merged or split in transit, so a reader must frame messages itself.
Retransmission can take seconds or minutes; TCP promises eventual in-order delivery, not a time bound.
Plain TCP is readable on the wire; TLS adds encryption on top.

qs.q: What does successful TLS certificate verification actually establish?
a: The server has the key for a cert naming this host, from a CA you trust
The site is legitimate and safe to give your personal details to
The connection is encrypted, which without verification would be plaintext
The server's software has been audited for known vulnerabilities
qs.e: Verification checks a chain of signatures from the server's certificate up to a root in your trust store, that the certificate names the host you asked for, and that it is in date; the handshake proves the server has the matching private key. That rules out a machine in the middle posing as the server. It says nothing about the owner's intentions, and any phishing domain can get a valid certificate.
explain_choice: CAs check control of the domain, not honesty; phishing sites routinely have valid certificates.
The traffic is encrypted either way; turning verification off leaves it encrypted to whoever answered, which is what a man-in-the-middle attack exploits.
A certificate says nothing about the server's patch level or code quality.

qs.q: Why add random jitter to exponential backoff?
a: So clients that failed together don't retry together
So each retry comes sooner and the call recovers faster
So retries slip under the server's rate limiter
So the request always succeeds if retried enough
qs.e: When a service fails, all its clients see the error at roughly the same moment. With plain exponential backoff they then retry at the same moments, 1 s, 2 s, 4 s later, in synchronised waves that can knock the recovering service over again. Randomising each delay (for example, uniform between 0 and the backoff cap) spreads the retries into a steady trickle.
explain_choice: Jitter can lengthen or shorten an individual delay; its purpose is to spread load, not to speed up recovery.
Rate limiters count requests per client, however they are timed; jitter is about protecting the server, not evading it.
Retries cannot fix a permanent error such as a 400; backoff needs a cap on attempts or on total time.

qs.q: WebSockets beat periodic polling when:
a: The server must push frequent updates with low delay
Updates are rare, a few times a day at most
Responses should be cached by browsers and CDNs
Each client sends one request and needs exactly one reply back
qs.e: Polling asks 'anything new?' on a timer, so you choose between delay (a long interval) and wasted requests (a short one). A WebSocket keeps one connection open, and the server writes to it the moment something happens. That only pays off when updates are frequent enough to justify the held connection; rare updates are cheaper to poll.
explain_choice: For rare updates, an idle connection per client for hours costs more than an occasional poll.
WebSocket frames bypass HTTP caching entirely; cacheable data suits plain GET requests.
One request with one reply is exactly what plain HTTP is for; a persistent socket adds cost and nothing else.

qs.q: Your page's `fetch()` to another origin fails with a CORS error. Where is that rule enforced?
a: In the browser, based on headers in the server's response
On the server, which refuses to answer requests from other origins
In a firewall or proxy between the page and the API
In every HTTP client, including curl and requests
qs.e: The same-origin policy is a browser rule that protects the user's cookies and sessions from other sites' scripts. For a simple request the browser sends it, reads the response's Access-Control-Allow-Origin, and hides the body from the page if the origin is not allowed. So the server may well have done the work. curl and requests have no such policy, which is why the call works from a terminal.
explain_choice: The server only states a policy in its headers; the request often reaches it and is processed, and it is the browser that withholds the response.
No network device takes part; the check happens inside the browser after the response arrives.
Command-line clients ignore CORS entirely, which is why the same request succeeds from a terminal.

qs.q: Your dev server listens on 127.0.0.1:8000. A phone on the same Wi-Fi can't reach it at your laptop's IP. Why?
a: 127.0.0.1 is loopback, which only accepts connections from this machine
Port 8000 is reserved for local use and can't be reached remotely
127.0.0.1 is the router's address, so the phone's requests are sent there
Phones can only reach servers over HTTPS on port 443
qs.e: A listening socket is bound to one address. The loopback interface never carries traffic from other machines, so a server bound to 127.0.0.1 is unreachable from the network whatever the firewall says. Bind to 0.0.0.0, meaning all interfaces, or to the laptop's LAN address, and then check the firewall.
explain_choice: Ports above 1023 are unprivileged and have no local-only rule; what makes it local is the address the socket is bound to.
127.0.0.1 is every machine's own loopback address; the router has an ordinary LAN address, often 192.168.x.1.
Phones can make plain HTTP requests to any port; the refusal comes from the bind address.

qs.q: You change a DNS A record, but an hour later some users still reach the old server. Why?
a: Resolvers and clients cache the old record until its TTL runs out
Every root server must copy your change, which takes up to 72 hours
DNS changes go out to all resolvers in one nightly batch
The old server still holds the certificate, so traffic sticks to it
qs.e: A resolver that looked up your name keeps the answer for the record's TTL, and operating systems, browsers and language runtimes may cache it too; some keep it longer than the TTL. Nothing is pushed out: each cache expires on its own clock. Lowering the TTL a day before a planned move keeps the switch short.
explain_choice: Root servers only point to the servers for each top-level domain; your record lives on your own authoritative servers and is never copied to the roots.
There is no push or batch; each cache holds the answer until its TTL expires, then asks again.
Certificates play no part in choosing an IP address; the client connects to whatever address its cached DNS answer gives.

qs.q: `requests.get(url, timeout=10)` hits a server that sends one byte every five seconds, forever. What happens?
a: It never times out, since 10 s bounds each wait for data
It raises Timeout once 10 seconds of total elapsed time have passed
It returns the partial body after 10 seconds
It raises at once, since the reads are too slow
qs.e: In requests the timeout applies to the connect and then to each wait for the next bytes on the socket, not to the whole call. A trickle that never pauses for 10 seconds resets the clock on every byte, so the call runs indefinitely. A real budget needs an overall deadline, for example streaming the body and checking elapsed time, or an HTTP client with a total timeout.
explain_choice: requests has no total-time timeout; the number bounds each read, so a slow but steady server never trips it.
requests has no 'return what you have' behaviour; a timeout raises an exception.
Slowness alone does not trigger it; only a gap longer than the timeout between bytes does.

qs.q: A session cookie is set with the HttpOnly flag. What does that protect against?
a: Page JavaScript reading it, so an XSS bug can't simply steal it
Being sent over plain HTTP, where anyone on the network could read it
Being attached to requests that other sites trigger
The user editing its value in their own browser
qs.e: HttpOnly hides the cookie from `document.cookie` and other script APIs while the browser still sends it with requests. That removes the easiest payoff of an XSS bug, copying the session token to an attacker. Each of the other threats has its own flag or defence: Secure for plain HTTP, SameSite for cross-site requests, and a server-side signature for tampering.
explain_choice: That is the Secure flag, which keeps the cookie off unencrypted connections.
That is the SameSite attribute, the main browser-side defence against CSRF.
Users can always edit their own cookies; only a server-side signature or lookup detects tampering.

qs.q: `authors LEFT JOIN books ON books.author_id = authors.id` returns:
a: Every author, once per matching book, with NULLs where there is none
Only the authors who have at least one matching book
Every author and every book, NULL-filled on either side
Every author exactly once, with at most one matching book beside each
qs.e: A left join starts from the inner join, where each author is repeated once per matching book, then adds back every author with no match, padding the book columns with NULL. So an author with three books appears three times. A WHERE clause on a books column, such as `WHERE books.year > 2000`, discards those NULL rows and quietly turns it back into an inner join.
explain_choice: That is an inner join; a left join keeps the unmatched left rows too.
Keeping unmatched rows from both sides is a FULL OUTER JOIN.
Joins never collapse matches: an author with three books appears on three rows.

qs.q: An index speeds up reads. What does it cost?
a: Slower writes and more storage, since each write updates it too
Nothing once built, since the planner simply skips it when it doesn't help
Just disk space; inserts and updates run at the same speed
Slower reads on other columns, which must scan around it
qs.e: An index is a second sorted structure that must stay consistent with the table, so every INSERT, every DELETE and any UPDATE of an indexed column also modifies each index, and every index takes space on disk and in cache. Ten unused indexes on a busy table can make writes several times slower for no gain.
explain_choice: The planner can ignore an index on reads, but writes must still maintain it; that cost never goes away.
Every insert and delete touches every index on the table, so writes slow down as indexes accumulate.
An index on one column does not change how other columns are read; its cost falls on writes and space.

qs.q: Does a B-tree index on `(a, b)` help `WHERE b = 5` when the query doesn't mention `a`?
a: Usually not: entries are ordered by a first, and by b only within each a
Yes, a composite index serves a lookup on any one of its columns equally
Yes, but only if b has fewer distinct values than a
No, and it can't serve `WHERE a = 5` on its own either
qs.e: A composite index is ordered like a phone book by surname, then first name: all b = 5 entries are scattered across every value of a, so there is no contiguous range to jump to. Filtering on a alone, or on a and b, uses the ordering directly. Some engines can use a skip scan, including PostgreSQL 18, but that only pays off when a has few distinct values.
explain_choice: The sort order is by a first, so only a leading prefix of the columns can be searched as a range.
It is the leading column's distinct count that matters, and only for engines with skip scan; with few values of a they can visit each one.
A leading prefix is exactly what a composite index serves well; `WHERE a = 5` uses it directly.

qs.q: What does a transaction's atomicity guarantee?
a: All of its changes take effect, or none of them do
Other sessions can't see its changes until it commits
Its committed changes survive a crash or power loss
It runs as if no other transaction ran at the same time
qs.e: Atomicity is the A in ACID: if any statement fails, or the connection drops before COMMIT, the database rolls back everything the transaction did, so a transfer never debits one account without crediting the other. Visibility to other sessions is isolation, and surviving a crash is durability; they are separate guarantees with separate settings.
explain_choice: Hiding uncommitted changes from others is isolation, the I in ACID.
Surviving a crash after commit is durability, the D in ACID, provided by the write-ahead log.
Behaving as if run alone is serializability, the strictest isolation level, which most databases do not use by default.

qs.q: Transaction A holds a lock B needs, while B holds a lock A needs. What happens in PostgreSQL?
a: It detects the deadlock and aborts one of them with an error
Both wait until the statement timeout, if one has been set
The database merges both into one transaction and commits it
The second writer wins, and the first writer's update is lost
qs.e: Neither can proceed, so the database checks for a cycle in its lock waits (after deadlock_timeout, one second by default) and aborts one transaction with a deadlock error, releasing its locks so the other finishes. Your code must catch that error and retry the whole transaction. Taking locks in a consistent order, such as by ascending id, prevents it.
explain_choice: PostgreSQL does not rely on a timeout; its deadlock detector breaks the cycle within about a second.
Transactions are never merged; one is chosen as the victim and rolled back.
A lost update is a different problem that happens without any lock wait; here both are blocked.

qs.q: What is the N+1 query problem?
a: Fetching a list, then running one more query per item for related data
Adding one index too many, so every write updates N+1 indexes
Forgetting a WHERE clause, so a query reads N+1 rows too many
A join that duplicates each row once per extra matching child
qs.e: An ORM that loads relations lazily runs one query for the list and then, when your loop touches `book.author`, one query per book: 1 + N round trips, each with its own network and parse cost. It is invisible in a unit test with three rows and slow in production. Eager loading (a join, or one IN query per relation) makes it a constant number of queries.
explain_choice: It is about the number of queries sent, not the number of indexes.
A missing WHERE reads too much data in one query; N+1 is many small queries.
Row duplication from a join is a separate effect; N+1 is what happens when you avoid the join.

qs.q: What does `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` give you that plain `EXPLAIN` does not?
a: It runs the query and reports real row counts and timings per step
It recommends the indexes that would make the query faster
It checks the syntax and refreshes the table's statistics
It shows the plan the planner would choose, without running the query
qs.e: EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan with the planner's estimates. ANALYZE also executes it and shows the actual rows and time at each node, so you can spot where estimates diverge from reality, often the real cause of a bad plan. Because it executes the query, wrap an UPDATE or DELETE in BEGIN ... ROLLBACK.
explain_choice: PostgreSQL recommends nothing; you read the plan and decide on an index yourself.
Refreshing statistics is the separate ANALYZE command; EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query.
That is what plain EXPLAIN does; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query.

qs.q: What does a foreign key constraint mainly give you?
a: The database refuses rows that point at a parent that doesn't exist
Faster joins, because the referencing column gets indexed automatically
Deleting a parent row deletes its child rows automatically
A relationship the ORM can follow without extra configuration
qs.e: The constraint makes the database check every insert and update on the child, and every delete of a parent, so orphaned rows cannot exist however many code paths write to the tables. It does not index the referencing column in PostgreSQL, so add one yourself if you join or delete by it. Cascading deletes happen only with ON DELETE CASCADE.
explain_choice: PostgreSQL indexes the referenced key but not the referencing column; MySQL's InnoDB creates one, which is where the belief comes from.
The default action is to reject the delete; cascading needs ON DELETE CASCADE.
ORMs declare relationships in their own models; the constraint is about the database enforcing integrity.

qs.q: Why does a web app need a database connection pool?
a: New connections are slow to open, and servers cap how many can exist
A pool caches query results, so repeated reads skip the database
Pooled connections are encrypted, whereas one-off connections are not
A pool lets one connection run several queries in parallel
qs.e: Each new PostgreSQL connection costs a TCP handshake, often TLS, authentication and a new server process. Servers cap the total (max_connections, 100 by default). A pool keeps a few connections open and lends them out per request, so under load you queue for a connection instead of exhausting the server's limit.
explain_choice: Pools reuse connections, not results; every query still runs on the server.
Encryption is set per connection (TLS) and is unrelated to pooling.
A connection runs one query at a time; a pool gives concurrency by holding several connections.

qs.q: To list customers with more than five orders, why does `WHERE COUNT(*) > 5` fail?
a: WHERE filters rows before grouping, so no count exists yet
COUNT(*) includes NULLs, so a WHERE needs COUNT(id)
WHERE can't reference columns that aren't in the SELECT list
It works, but linters reject it because HAVING is the faster form
qs.e: A query is evaluated FROM, then WHERE on individual rows, then GROUP BY, then HAVING on each group, then SELECT. An aggregate only has a value once rows are grouped, so the condition belongs in HAVING: `GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 5`. Row filters that do not need an aggregate stay in WHERE, where they shrink the input before grouping.
explain_choice: The NULL handling of COUNT is unrelated; any aggregate in WHERE is an error because grouping has not happened yet.
WHERE can use any column of the FROM tables; the problem is the aggregate, not the column list.
It is not a style warning; SQL rejects aggregates in WHERE with an error.

qs.q: `email` is indexed, yet `WHERE lower(email) = 'a@b.com'` does a full table scan. Why?
a: The index is on email, not lower(email), so it can't be searched
B-tree indexes suit numeric columns, not text columns like email
Equality on strings needs a hash index rather than a B-tree
Wrapping a column in any function in WHERE disables every index on the table
qs.e: The index stores email values sorted as written, and the planner cannot search it for the result of lower() without computing lower() for every row. Either create an expression index, `CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email))`, or store the email in a normalised form and compare it directly. Other indexes on the table are unaffected.
explain_choice: B-trees order text perfectly well; the problem is that the query asks about a different expression.
B-trees handle equality as well as ranges; a hash index would have the same problem with lower().
Only the wrapped column loses its index; an expression index on the same function is used normally.

qs.q: In PostgreSQL at the default READ COMMITTED level, two transactions both run `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1`. What happens?
a: The second waits for the lock, then subtracts from the updated balance
Both read the old balance, so one of the two deductions is silently lost
The second fails with a serialization error and must be retried
They deadlock, and the database aborts one of them
qs.e: The first UPDATE takes a row lock. The second blocks on it, and once the first commits it re-reads the latest version of the row and subtracts from that, so both deductions apply. Lost updates happen when the application reads the balance, computes in Python and writes back an absolute value; keeping the arithmetic in SQL, or using SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, avoids them.
explain_choice: That is the read-modify-write pattern done in application code; a single UPDATE re-checks the row after waiting for the lock.
Serialization failures come from REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE; READ COMMITTED waits and re-reads instead.
A deadlock needs two locks taken in opposite orders; here both want the same single row lock, so one simply waits.

qs.q: Why can a CTE (`WITH ...`) be slow in PostgreSQL 11 but fast in 12 and later?
a: Before 12 CTEs were always materialised, so outer filters couldn't reach in
Before 12 a CTE was re-run once for every row of the query that referenced it
From 12, CTE results are cached across queries and sessions
From 12, indexes are no longer allowed inside a CTE
qs.e: Up to version 11 a CTE was an optimisation fence: it was computed in full into a temporary result, so a later `WHERE id = 5` could not be pushed into it to use an index. Since 12, a non-recursive, side-effect-free CTE referenced once is inlined like a subquery. `AS MATERIALIZED` and `AS NOT MATERIALIZED` let you choose explicitly.
explain_choice: That describes a correlated subquery; a CTE was computed once per query, which was the problem.
PostgreSQL has no cross-query result cache; each query computes its CTEs afresh.
Indexes are used inside CTEs in every version; the change was about inlining.

qs.q: Why does `SELECT * FROM users WHERE deleted_at = NULL` return no rows, even for users never deleted?
a: Comparing anything with = NULL gives unknown, never true; use IS NULL
It matches only rows where the column holds the text 'NULL'
NULL can't be compared at all, so the query errors out and returns nothing
It matches only rows inserted after the column was added
qs.e: SQL uses three-valued logic: NULL means 'unknown', so `x = NULL` evaluates to unknown for every x, including NULL itself, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true. `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL` are the tests for missing values. The same logic makes `NOT IN (subquery)` return nothing if the subquery yields a NULL.
explain_choice: The literal NULL is not a string; comparing with the text 'NULL' would be `= 'NULL'`.
The query runs without error; each comparison is simply unknown, so no row passes.
Rows added before the column exists hold NULL like any other; the comparison fails for them all equally.

qs.q: How do authentication and authorisation differ?
a: Authentication establishes who you are; authorisation, what you may do
Authentication proves identity to users; authorisation proves it to APIs
Authorisation checks the password; authentication then checks the role
They are the same check, both done by the login middleware
qs.e: Authentication answers 'who is this?' once per request, from a password, token or certificate. Authorisation then answers 'may this identity do this to this object?', a separate decision that depends on the resource. The two fail independently: a flawless login does nothing to stop user 7 fetching `/invoices/8`, and broken object-level authorisation is the most common API vulnerability.
explain_choice: Both apply to any caller, human or machine; the split is identity versus permission, not audience.
That reverses them: checking a password is authentication, and roles and permissions are authorisation.
Login middleware establishes identity only; whether that identity may touch a given object is checked separately.

qs.q: Where must access control be enforced?
a: Always on the server, for each request and each object touched
In the frontend, by hiding what the user may not use
Once at login, then trusted for the rest of the user's session
At the API gateway only, so handlers can stay simple
qs.e: Anyone can send HTTP requests with curl, skipping your UI entirely, and change an ID in the URL. So the server must check, on each request, that this user may perform this action on this specific object. A gateway can reject unauthenticated traffic, but it does not know who owns invoice 8; only the code that loads the invoice does.
explain_choice: Hiding buttons is good UX but no protection: the request can be crafted directly without the page.
Permissions change and objects differ per request; a login proves identity, not the right to each resource.
A gateway can check the token but not object-level ownership, which needs the application's data.

qs.q: What is the main trade-off of a stateless JWT compared with a server-side session?
a: It can't easily be revoked before expiry, as the server keeps no record
It is encrypted, so the client can't read the claims inside it
It has to be looked up in the database on every request
It works on a single server, where sessions scale out
qs.e: The server trusts a JWT because its signature checks out, so nothing needs to be looked up, and that is also why it cannot be cancelled: a stolen token stays valid until `exp`. Short-lived access tokens plus revocable refresh tokens, or a denylist, recover some control. Signed JWTs are only base64url-encoded, so anyone holding one can read its claims.
explain_choice: A standard signed JWT (JWS) is readable by anyone who base64-decodes it; never put secrets in its claims.
Avoiding a per-request lookup is the whole point of a self-contained token; the cost is revocation.
It is sessions that need shared storage to work across servers; any server with the key can verify a JWT.

qs.q: How should passwords be stored?
a: With a slow, salted password hash such as argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt
As SHA-256 with a per-user salt, since the salt defeats rainbow tables
Encrypted with AES, the key kept in an environment variable
As SHA-512, since a longer hash takes longer to brute-force
qs.e: An attacker who steals the table tries guesses offline, so what matters is the cost per guess. A salt only stops precomputed tables and identical passwords sharing a hash; SHA-256 is designed to be fast, billions per second on a GPU. Password hashes are tuned to be slow, and argon2id and scrypt also make each guess need lots of memory, which defeats GPUs.
explain_choice: Salting blocks rainbow tables, but a fast hash still lets an attacker test billions of guesses per second.
Encryption is reversible: whoever gets the key, often from the same server, gets every password.
Digest length has little effect on guessing cost; SHA-512 is still built to be fast.

qs.q: Why does `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000` pagination break down on large tables?
a: The database reads and discards every skipped row, and rows shift as data changes
OFFSET needs an index on the sort column, so it fails on unindexed tables
SQL doesn't guarantee OFFSET works together with an ORDER BY clause
Clients can't jump straight to a page number, as they can with cursor pagination
qs.e: OFFSET is not a seek: to skip 100,000 rows the database produces them in order and throws them away, so page 5,000 costs far more than page 1. And if a row is inserted or deleted before the current page between requests, items move across page boundaries and get repeated or skipped. Cursor (keyset) pagination, `WHERE (created, id) > (:last_created, :last_id)`, seeks straight to the position through an index.
explain_choice: OFFSET works without an index; it is just slow either way at depth, because the skipped rows are still produced.
OFFSET with ORDER BY is standard and deterministic when the sort key is unique; the problems are cost and drift.
That reverses them: jumping to page N is offset's strength and cursor pagination's limitation.

qs.q: What do Pydantic models in a FastAPI route mainly give you?
a: Parsed, validated request and response data, plus the OpenAPI schema
Faster routing, since the models are compiled into native code
Database access, since each model maps to a table like an ORM
Authentication, since the model checks the fields of the caller's token
qs.e: FastAPI reads the type hints on your route, parses the body and parameters with Pydantic, rejects bad input with a 422 listing each field error, and filters output through the response model. The same models produce the OpenAPI schema and the /docs page. So the handler's body can trust the shape of its data.
explain_choice: pydantic-core is written in Rust, but that speeds up validation; route matching is Starlette's job and unrelated.
Pydantic models are not tied to tables; SQLModel combines the two, but Pydantic alone does no persistence.
Authentication is handled by security dependencies; a model can describe a token's shape but checks no credentials.

qs.q: What does putting a request ID on every log line let you do?
a: Pull out every line for one request from many interleaved ones
Sort log lines back into the order that requests arrived
Drop duplicate retries, since a retried request keeps its original ID
Rate-limit each client by counting its request IDs
qs.e: Under concurrency, lines from dozens of requests interleave in one stream, so 'the error after the query' may belong to a different user. Middleware generates or accepts an ID, stores it in a contextvar, and the log formatter adds it to every line, including lines from downstream services if you forward the header. Filtering on one ID reconstructs one request's path.
explain_choice: Timestamps order lines; the ID groups them by request, which a timestamp cannot.
Each attempt usually gets a new request ID; recognising a duplicate is the job of an idempotency key.
Rate limiting counts by client identity, such as a key or IP; a request ID is unique per request.

qs.q: Is returning a stack trace in an API error response acceptable in production?
a: Never: it leaks paths, versions and code that help an attacker map the system
Yes, if the API is only called by your own frontend and never by users
Yes, once the service is behind HTTPS, as nobody else can read it
Yes, because users can include it in the bug reports they send you
qs.e: A trace shows file paths, library versions, SQL fragments and the shape of your code, a free reconnaissance report for the person causing errors on purpose. Log it server-side with a correlation ID and return a generic message containing that ID; support can then find the full trace without exposing it.
explain_choice: Anyone can call the API directly, bypassing your frontend, and see the same response.
HTTPS hides it from eavesdroppers, but the attacker is the client receiving the response.
An error ID in the response gives support the same trace from the logs without handing it to every caller.

qs.q: Why is running background work inside the web process (such as FastAPI's BackgroundTasks) risky for important jobs?
a: Queued work lives in memory and is lost when the process stops or crashes
The response is held back until every background task has finished
Background tasks can no longer write to the logs once the request has ended
A second worker process is needed for them to run at all
qs.e: In-process tasks run after the response is sent, in the same process, with no record anywhere else. A deploy, an autoscaler removing the instance or an out-of-memory kill takes pending work with it, and nothing retries it. Work that must happen, such as sending a receipt, belongs in a durable queue whose worker acknowledges a job only after it completes.
explain_choice: FastAPI sends the response first and then runs the tasks; the problem is durability, not latency.
Logging works as normal in background tasks; only the request's own scope has ended.
They run in the same process with no extra worker, which is exactly why a restart loses them.

qs.q: A FastAPI route declares `db = Depends(get_db)`. How should a test make it use a test database?
a: Put a test-session function in `app.dependency_overrides[get_db]`
Monkeypatch `get_db` in its own module after the app has been imported
Set an environment variable that `get_db` reads when first imported
Pass the test session as a query parameter named `db` in the request
qs.e: Depends stores a reference to the get_db function object when the route is defined, and FastAPI looks up overrides by that same object. Rebinding the module attribute later changes nothing the route holds. dependency_overrides swaps it where FastAPI resolves dependencies; clear it after each test.
explain_choice: The route captured the original function object when it was defined, so rebinding the name in the module has no effect.
A value read at import time is fixed before the test can set it; overrides act at request time instead.
Dependencies are not request parameters; a client cannot supply them.

qs.q: `alembic revision --autogenerate` has written a migration. What next?
a: Read and edit it; it misses some changes and turns renames into drop-and-add
Apply it straight away, since it was generated from the models and must be right
Delete it and call `create_all()`, which does the same thing more simply
Commit it unread, since CI applies every migration in order anyway
qs.e: Autogenerate diffs your models against the live schema. It cannot tell a renamed column from a dropped column plus a new one, which would destroy the data, and it misses some changes such as certain constraint and server-default edits. It also writes no data migrations. Treat its output as a draft to review.
explain_choice: It compares structure, not intent: a renamed column appears as a drop and an add, and running that loses the column's data.
create_all only creates missing tables; it never alters existing ones, and it keeps no version history.
CI running it in order does not make a wrong migration right; the data loss just happens in every environment.

qs.q: Your API tests pass one at a time but fail when the whole suite runs. The usual cause is:
a: The tests share database state, so one test's rows leak into the next
pytest runs the tests in parallel by default, and they collide
The test client caches responses between the tests that use it
Fixtures get rebuilt for every single test, which makes later tests time out
qs.e: A test that inserts a user and never cleans up changes what the next test's queries return, so results depend on order. The standard fix is to run each test inside a transaction that is rolled back at teardown, or use a fresh database per test, so every test starts from the same state.
explain_choice: pytest runs tests serially unless you add a plugin such as pytest-xdist.
The test client does not cache responses; each call goes through the app.
Function-scoped fixtures being rebuilt is what gives isolation; it makes tests slower, not wrong.

qs.q: How should an upload endpoint decide whether a file is an acceptable image?
a: Cap the size while reading, then check the bytes themselves
Trust the Content-Type header that the browser sent along with the file
Check the filename's extension against an allow-list of image types
Rely on the form's `accept=` attribute to stop other file types
qs.e: Everything the client sends about the file, including name, extension and Content-Type, is chosen by the client and can say anything. The server should stop reading past a size limit, so a 10 GB upload cannot fill the disk, then check the bytes: magic numbers at minimum, or actually decoding the image. Store it under a generated name, never the one supplied.
explain_choice: The Content-Type is set by the client and can be any string an attacker likes.
Renaming `payload.exe` to `cat.png` takes a second; the extension says nothing about the content.
`accept=` only filters the browser's file picker; a direct request ignores it.

QUIZZES.d: Work that runs while you sleep.

qs.q: A setup job creates folders, writes a config file and registers a webhook. Which step design keeps a second run harmless?
a: Each step checks the current state and acts only to reach the target
Each step writes a 'done' marker before it starts, then does its work
The whole job is wrapped in try/except so reruns can't fail
The scheduler guarantees it fires once, so reruns can't happen
qs.e: A convergent step describes an end state rather than an action: `mkdir(exist_ok=True)`, write the config only if it differs, look up the webhook before creating it. Run it once or five times and the system ends up the same, which covers manual reruns, crashes part way through and a scheduler firing twice. Marking a step done before doing it gives the opposite: a crash between the two leaves the work skipped forever.
explain_choice: If the job crashes after writing the marker and before the work, reruns skip that step for good; a marker belongs after the work.
Swallowing exceptions hides failures; the second run still creates a duplicate webhook, it just does so silently.
Schedulers do fire twice (retries, failovers, clock changes), and people rerun jobs by hand; the job itself must tolerate it.

qs.q: Your scraper breaks every week or two. What is the most likely cause?
a: Its selectors rely on generated class names or deep layout paths
The site rate-limits it, which returns an empty page instead of data
The parsing library changes its API in each minor release
The site blocks the scraper's User-Agent string each week
qs.e: Front-end build tools generate class names such as `.css-1x7fq2` that change on every deploy, and paths like `div > div:nth-child(3) > span` break whenever a wrapper is added. Anchor on things the site keeps stable for its own reasons, such as ids, `data-*` attributes, ARIA labels or visible text, and make the scraper fail loudly when an expected field is missing rather than saving blanks.
explain_choice: Rate limiting shows up as 429 responses or blocks, usually immediately, not as a weekly selector failure.
Parsers such as BeautifulSoup and lxml keep stable APIs; weekly breakage tracks the site's deploys, not library releases.
A blocked User-Agent gives 403s or captchas; a changed page with a 200 status points at the markup.

qs.q: An API answers 429 Too Many Requests. What should your client do?
a: Wait before retrying, using the Retry-After value when it is sent
Retry at once, since 429 just means the server is busy for now
Switch to another IP address so the limit no longer applies
Drop the task as a permanent failure and move on to the next
qs.e: 429 is the server telling you to slow down. Retry-After, when present, says how many seconds (or until what date) to wait; otherwise back off exponentially with jitter. Then lower your sending rate, because a client that keeps hitting the limit tends to get blocked for longer. The task itself is still valid and should be retried, not dropped.
explain_choice: Retrying at once is precisely what the limit is there to stop, and repeated violations often escalate to longer blocks.
Rotating IPs to dodge a limit is evasion that breaks most terms of service and gets keys revoked.
The request was fine; it needs to be sent later, not discarded.

qs.q: When do you need Playwright rather than a plain HTTP client like requests?
a: When the content is built by JavaScript after the page's HTML loads
When the site sets cookies, which requests can't keep between calls
When the site is slow, since a browser waits more patiently for it
When the page is very large, since a browser streams it more efficiently
qs.e: An HTTP client receives the initial HTML and runs no scripts, so anything the page fetches and renders with JavaScript is missing. A real browser executes those scripts. Before reaching for one, check the network tab: the page often loads its data from a JSON endpoint you can call directly, which is faster and far more stable.
explain_choice: `requests.Session()` stores and resends cookies automatically; cookies alone do not need a browser.
Timeouts are configurable in any client; a browser is slower and heavier, not more patient.
A full browser downloads and renders far more than the HTML; for a large static page an HTTP client is cheaper.

qs.q: What should a webhook receiver do when a delivery arrives?
a: Verify the signature, queue the work, and return 2xx quickly
Do all the work first, then respond, so the sender knows it worked
Skip signature checks, since the endpoint URL is kept secret
Call the sender's API to confirm the event before replying
qs.e: Senders wait only a few seconds and then treat the delivery as failed and send it again, so slow inline processing causes duplicates. Verifying the HMAC signature over the raw body proves the sender and the content; then persist the event, reply 2xx and process from the queue, deduplicating on the event ID because retries still happen.
explain_choice: Long processing risks the sender's timeout, which triggers a redelivery and duplicate work.
URLs leak through logs, proxies and screenshots; the signature is what proves who sent it.
An extra API call before replying adds latency and a new failure point; the signature already proves authenticity.

qs.q: What should you check before scraping a site?
a: Its terms of service, robots.txt, and whether an official API exists
Only robots.txt, since that file is what grants legal permission to scrape
Nothing, if the data is publicly visible without logging in
That you send a realistic browser User-Agent so you blend in
qs.e: An official API is usually faster, more stable and explicitly allowed. The terms of service set what the owner permits, and robots.txt says which paths automated clients should avoid; neither alone is the whole picture, and both affect whether you keep access. Rate-limit yourself and identify your client honestly.
explain_choice: robots.txt is a convention for crawlers, not a licence; the terms of service and applicable law still apply.
Being publicly viewable does not grant permission for automated copying; terms and rate limits still apply.
Disguising the client is the opposite of respectful crawling and often breaches the terms.

qs.q: A job crashes after processing 6,000 of 10,000 items. What does good design let you do?
a: Resume from saved progress, skipping items already completed
Start over, since partial results from a crash can't be trusted
Rerun with smaller batches, so the next crash loses less work
Retry the whole job in a loop until one full run completes
qs.e: If each item's completion is recorded durably, in the same transaction as its result or right after an idempotent write, the rerun reads that record and continues from item 6,001. Starting over repeats work and side effects such as emails, and whole-job retries do the same on every failure. Checkpointing is what turns a crash into a short delay.
explain_choice: Results committed per item are trustworthy; redoing them repeats side effects such as emails or charges.
Smaller batches reduce what one crash loses, but without saved progress you still restart from the beginning.
Each retry redoes all the completed items, and a persistent failure loops forever.

qs.q: Where should an automation script's API keys and passwords live?
a: In environment variables or a secret manager, kept out of Git
In the script, since the repository is private to you
In the source, base64-encoded so a quick glance can't read them
In a `.env` file committed so teammates can run the script
qs.e: Anything committed stays in the repository's history, which is cloned, forked, backed up and sometimes made public. Deleting the line later does not remove it. Load secrets at run time from the environment or a secret manager, keep `.env` in .gitignore, and rotate any key that was ever committed.
explain_choice: Private repositories get shared, forked, made public and cloned onto laptops; the secret is in every copy of the history.
base64 is an encoding, not encryption; anyone can decode it in one command.
A committed .env is a committed secret; share an example file with placeholders instead.

qs.q: A Playwright script sometimes fails to click a button that appears after a request. What is the robust fix?
a: Use locator actions that auto-wait, or wait for a specific condition
Add `time.sleep(5)` before the click to give the page time
Run the browser headed, since headless mode skips drawing some buttons
Rerun the whole script automatically until one attempt succeeds
qs.e: Timing varies from run to run, so a fixed sleep is either too short on a slow day or wasted time on a fast one. Playwright's locator actions wait until the element is attached, visible, stable and enabled before acting, and `expect(...)` or `wait_for_response` waits for a named condition. Waiting on the condition you actually need removes the race rather than guessing its length.
explain_choice: A sleep guesses a duration; it still fails on a slow run and slows every fast one.
Headless browsers render the same DOM; differences come from viewport size or timing, not skipped elements.
Retrying hides a race rather than fixing it, and repeats side effects of the earlier steps.

qs.q: Your job's OAuth access token expires after an hour, but the job runs for six. What should it do?
a: Use the refresh token to get a new access token when it expires
Store the user's password and log in again every hour
Request a token with no expiry, which most servers grant if you ask for one
Keep using the old token, since expiry is just a suggestion
qs.e: OAuth separates a short-lived access token, sent with every call, from a longer-lived refresh token, sent only to the token endpoint. When the access token expires, or a call returns 401, exchange the refresh token for a new pair and retry once. Store the refresh token as a secret, and save the new one if the server rotates it.
explain_choice: Holding the password defeats the point of OAuth, and many providers do not allow a password grant at all.
Lifetimes are the provider's policy; a client cannot ask for a token that never expires.
The resource server checks `exp` and rejects expired tokens with 401.

qs.q: A job scheduled every five minutes sometimes takes seven. What stops two copies running at once?
a: Take an exclusive lock at start, such as flock, and exit if it is held
Nothing is needed: cron waits for one run to finish before starting the next
Check `ps` at start for another process with the script's name
Move the schedule to every ten minutes so the runs can't overlap
qs.e: cron starts each run on the clock whether or not the last one has finished. An atomic lock taken at start, such as `flock -n /tmp/job.lock` or a database advisory lock, lets exactly one run proceed, and the operating system releases it if the holder dies. A check followed by a separate start leaves a window in which both runs pass the check.
explain_choice: cron has no idea a previous run is still going; it starts a new one every time the schedule matches.
Two runs can both check `ps` before either appears in it; the check and the claim must be one atomic step.
A longer interval only moves the problem: the day the job takes eleven minutes, runs overlap again.

qs.q: An API response carries `Link: <https://api.example.com/items?cursor=abc>; rel="next"`. How should you page through the results?
a: Follow the rel="next" URL each time until a response has none
Increment a page number yourself until a page comes back empty
Read the total count and build every page URL before you start
Pass page=all to fetch every result in a single request
qs.e: The server hands you the exact URL of the next page, often with an opaque cursor, so the client does not need to know how pagination works. Stop when no rel="next" is present. Building URLs yourself breaks when the API uses cursors, and it skips or repeats items when data changes mid-walk. requests exposes the parsed header as `response.links`.
explain_choice: The URL carries a cursor, not a page number; guessing numbers breaks as soon as the API changes scheme.
Counts go stale while you page, and a cursor-based API cannot be addressed by page number at all.
APIs cap page size to protect themselves; there is no standard page=all.

QUIZZES.d: Choosing a concurrency model and proving it.

qs.q: On the default (GIL-enabled) CPython build, what does the GIL stop?
a: Two threads in one process running Python bytecode at the same instant
Threads from overlapping at all, so threading gives no speed-up on I/O waits
Data races in your code, so a shared counter needs no lock around it
Several processes from running Python code on separate cores at once
qs.e: Only the thread holding the GIL may execute bytecode, but blocking I/O calls and many C extensions release it while they wait, so I/O-bound threads still overlap. It protects the interpreter's own state, not your invariants: a thread switch can still land between the steps of your own compound operation. Since 3.14 the free-threaded build (python3.14t, PEP 703, officially supported under PEP 779) has no GIL at all and runs bytecode in parallel, but the GIL build remains the default.
explain_choice: The GIL is released during blocking I/O, so threads waiting on sockets or files do overlap, which is why threads help I/O-bound work.
The GIL keeps CPython's internals consistent, not your data: `counter += 1` is several bytecodes and a switch can fall between them.
Each process has its own interpreter and its own GIL, so processes run truly in parallel; that is why multiprocessing exists.

qs.q: On the default CPython build, what makes pure-Python CPU-bound work use several cores?
a: Separate processes, or native code that releases the GIL while it computes
More threads, because the operating system gives each thread its own core
asyncio tasks, because the event loop spreads coroutines over the cores
A thread pool sized to match the core count, so that no core is left sitting idle
qs.e: Each process has its own interpreter and GIL, so the cores really run in parallel; the price is pickling arguments and results across the process boundary. Python 3.14 adds two more routes: per-interpreter GIL (PEP 684, in the C API since 3.12) exposed as `concurrent.interpreters` and `InterpreterPoolExecutor` (PEP 734), and the optional free-threaded build (PEP 703/779), where plain threads do run bytecode in parallel.
explain_choice: The OS will schedule threads on different cores, but on the GIL build only one of them can execute bytecode at a time, so the extra cores sit waiting.
An event loop runs on one thread; coroutines interleave at await points and never run at the same moment.
Pool size does not matter while every worker queues for the same GIL; a ThreadPoolExecutor only helps work that releases it.

qs.q: A coroutine reaches `await` on something that is not ready yet. What happens?
a: It suspends, and the event loop runs other ready tasks until it is able to resume
Its thread blocks until the result arrives, just like an ordinary call
The awaited call is handed to a worker thread from the default executor
The awaited call is scheduled, and the coroutine carries on to the next line
qs.e: A coroutine is a resumable function: at a suspension point it returns control to the loop, which picks another ready task on the same thread and resumes this one when its future completes. That is how one thread serves thousands of sockets, and why any call that blocks without awaiting freezes the whole loop.
explain_choice: Blocking the thread is exactly what await avoids; the loop's thread moves on to other tasks while this one waits.
Nothing moves to a thread unless you ask for it with asyncio.to_thread or run_in_executor; await alone stays on the loop's thread.
Execution does not continue past the await until the result is ready; to run something concurrently you create a task.

qs.q: What does calling `time.sleep(5)` inside an async function do?
a: Stalls every task on that event loop for the full five seconds
Pauses just this coroutine, the same way asyncio.sleep(5) would
Nothing harmful; asyncio patches it into a non-blocking sleep
Raises RuntimeError, since blocking calls are banned in coroutines
qs.e: time.sleep blocks the thread and never returns control to the loop, and every task on that loop shares the one thread, so none of them can run until it returns. Use `await asyncio.sleep(5)`, and push unavoidable blocking calls off the loop with `asyncio.to_thread`. Debug mode (PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1) logs callbacks that hog the loop, which is how you find these.
explain_choice: asyncio.sleep awaits a timer and yields to the loop; time.sleep holds the thread, so the whole loop stops with it.
asyncio does no monkey-patching of the standard library; that is gevent's approach, not asyncio's.
Python cannot tell a blocking call from any other call, so it runs silently; only debug mode warns you afterwards.

qs.q: You fire 10,000 requests at a third-party API with one unbounded `gather`. What is the likely result?
a: 429 responses, exhausted sockets, and possibly a blocked API key
It finishes about ten thousand times faster than a serial loop
Local memory grows, but the API still sees one request at a time
Nothing much, since asyncio caps concurrent tasks by default
qs.e: gather starts every coroutine at once, so every request is in flight together. Servers protect themselves with rate limits and bans, and your side runs out of sockets and file descriptors. An `asyncio.Semaphore` or a fixed pool of workers reading a queue bounds how many are in flight, which is what makes a concurrent client polite and predictable.
explain_choice: Speed-up stops at whatever the server or the network allows; past that, extra concurrency only adds errors and retries.
Every coroutine opens its own request as soon as gather schedules it, so the server sees them all at once.
asyncio puts no limit on tasks; any limit comes from the HTTP client's pool or from a semaphore you add yourself.

qs.q: What does `asyncio.TaskGroup` give you that a bare `asyncio.gather` does not?
a: When one child fails, the others are cancelled and all the errors raised together
The child tasks run truly in parallel, each on its own operating-system thread
Lower overhead, because it skips the scheduling step that gather performs
Results come back in completion order rather than in submission order
qs.e: This is structured concurrency: the `async with` block does not exit until every child has finished, and on the first failure it cancels the siblings and raises all failures as an ExceptionGroup, handled with `except*`. Plain gather (without return_exceptions) raises the first exception but leaves the other tasks running unsupervised, where they can leak work or hide more errors.
explain_choice: A TaskGroup runs its tasks on the same event loop thread as gather does; neither uses threads.
The benefit is about lifetime and error handling, not speed; both schedule tasks the same way.
Completion order is what asyncio.as_completed gives you; TaskGroup does not return results at all, you read them from the tasks.

qs.q: A nightly report takes twenty minutes. What should you do before changing any code?
a: Profile it, for example with cProfile, to see where the time actually goes
Rewrite the loop that looks slowest as a C extension, or with Cython
Put a cache in front of the database calls, since I/O is usually where the cost is
Spread the work over a thread pool, so all of the cores are kept busy
qs.e: Guesses about where time goes are wrong often enough that measuring first is cheaper than optimising the wrong thing. cProfile's cumulative-time view shows which call dominates; then change one thing and measure again, so every speed-up is a number rather than a feeling.
explain_choice: Rewriting code that turns out not to be the bottleneck costs days and changes nothing; the profile tells you where C would pay off.
Caching is a fix for one specific cause; if the time is spent in parsing or a quadratic loop, the cache does nothing.
Threads on the GIL build do not speed up CPU-bound Python, and without a profile you do not know the work is CPU-bound anyway.

qs.q: Why do latency targets usually quote p95 or p99 rather than the mean?
a: They show what the slowest 1 in 20 or 1 in 100 requests actually feel like
The mean is too expensive to calculate over millions of requests per minute
They are the mean with the outliers removed, so they are steadier over time
They measure how many requests per second the service is able to sustain
qs.e: A few slow requests barely move the mean, so the mean can look healthy while real users wait. Tails also compound: a page that makes 20 backend calls hits at least one p95-slow call on about 64 per cent of loads (1 - 0.95^20), so the tail becomes the typical user experience.
explain_choice: The mean is the cheapest statistic there is; percentiles are the costly ones, which is why tools use histograms to estimate them.
Percentiles keep the slow tail rather than trimming it; that tail is exactly what they are there to show.
That is throughput; latency percentiles describe how long individual requests take, not how many you can serve.

qs.q: Two threads each run `counter += 1` a million times on a shared global, with no lock. What can happen?
a: The total can come out short, because `+=` is a separate read, add and store
It stays exact, because the GIL turns each `+=` into one atomic bytecode step
It can go wrong on a machine with several cores, but not on a single core
It raises a RuntimeError when both threads write the variable at once
qs.e: Correctness now depends on timing: if a thread switch falls between one thread's read and its store, the other thread's update is overwritten and lost. The loss may be rare on your machine and common in production, which is why shared mutable state needs a Lock (or a design with no sharing) rather than trust in the scheduler.
explain_choice: The GIL protects single bytecodes, and `+=` on a global compiles to several; the switch can fall between them.
Interleaving only needs a thread switch, which a single core does constantly; more cores just change how often it bites.
Python raises nothing for unsynchronised access; the corruption is silent, which is what makes races hard to find.

qs.q: You cancel an asyncio task that holds a database connection. What must its code do?
a: Release it in a finally block, and re-raise CancelledError if the code catches it
Nothing: cancel() stops the task at once and frees everything it holds
Catch CancelledError and return normally, so the task ends without any error
Call loop.stop(), so no half-finished task is left running on the loop
qs.e: cancel() does not kill anything: it raises CancelledError inside the coroutine at its next await, and only code in `finally` (or an `async with` exit) runs on the way out. Swallowing the error makes the task look as if it finished normally, which breaks TaskGroup and asyncio.timeout, both of which rely on the cancellation propagating.
explain_choice: Cancellation is cooperative: it arrives as an exception at an await point, and anything not released in cleanup code leaks.
Swallowing CancelledError hides the cancellation from whoever asked for it; timeouts and task groups then misbehave.
Stopping the loop abandons every task mid-flight, which leaks far more than the one connection you were worried about.

qs.q: Why copy requirements.txt and run pip install before `COPY . .` in a Dockerfile?
a: A code edit then rebuilds from the source COPY onwards, reusing the install layer
It makes the final image smaller, because the install step skips the source
It changes nothing, since Docker caches every file by its name, whatever the order
Layers build in parallel, so putting the install first lets it start sooner
qs.e: Each instruction's cache entry depends on its inputs and on every layer before it, so the first changed layer invalidates everything after it. Source changes on every commit while dependencies rarely do; putting the stable, expensive step first means an ordinary edit costs seconds instead of a full reinstall.
explain_choice: Both orders put the same files and packages in the final image; the ordering affects rebuild time, not size.
The cache is keyed per instruction and chained; a changed COPY invalidates every instruction below it.
Classic Dockerfile steps within one stage run in order; only separate stages can build concurrently.

qs.q: Your image runs as root. What does adding a non-root USER actually buy you?
a: It limits what a code-execution bug in the container can reach
A smaller image, because root's home directory is left out of it
Faster start-up, because the kernel can skip its privilege checks
Volume mounts no longer need a chown on the host side
qs.e: Without user-namespace remapping, root in the container is uid 0 on the host kernel, so a container escape or a mounted host path becomes a root compromise. A non-root user turns a remote-code-execution bug into a much smaller incident, which is why isolation is treated as one layer rather than the whole defence.
explain_choice: The user an image runs as has no effect on its size; the layers are the same either way.
Privilege checks cost the same for every user; the change is about damage, not speed.
Ownership still has to match the uid the process runs as, so non-root often needs more chown work, not less.

qs.q: What does a multi-stage Docker build let you do?
a: Compile in a heavy build stage, then copy only the results into a slim one
Run all the build steps in parallel, so that the image finishes building sooner
Squash every layer into one, so the final image carries no history
Share one base layer between several services while they are running
qs.e: Only what you `COPY --from=` the build stage reaches the final image, so compilers, headers and pip caches stay behind in a stage that is thrown away. The result is smaller and has less attack surface, because tools an attacker could use were never shipped.
explain_choice: Independent stages can build concurrently, but that is a side effect; the point is leaving the toolchain out of what ships.
Squashing is a different feature; a multi-stage image still has layers, just none from the build stage.
Layer sharing between images happens through common base images, whether or not you use stages.

qs.q: A Postgres container is removed and recreated from the same image. When does its data survive?
a: When the data directory lives on a named volume or a bind mount
When you ran docker commit on the container before removing it
Every time, because the image keeps a copy of whatever was written
When the container ran as root, so it could write to the host disk
qs.e: Writes go to a thin writable layer that belongs to the container: a restart keeps it, but removal deletes it. Volumes are managed outside the container's lifecycle, so a new container that mounts the same volume sees the old data. That is why state must live in a volume or an external store.
explain_choice: commit snapshots the container's layer into a new image, but it never captures volumes, which is where the Postgres image keeps its data.
Images are read-only; each new container starts from the image's clean state, not from the last container's writes.
Running as root lets a process write inside the container, but the writable layer is still deleted with the container.

qs.q: What is a container health check for?
a: Letting the platform tell serving from merely running, and then act on the result
Restarting the container automatically whenever its main process exits
Exposing the service's port, so that other containers can reach it
Adding a start-up line to the logs, so you can see when it came up
qs.e: A process can be alive and still useless: deadlocked, out of connections, or failing every request. The check probes real behaviour, and orchestrators use the result: Compose's `depends_on: condition: service_healthy` waits for it, and Kubernetes readiness and liveness probes stop routing to, or restart, what fails. Plain Docker only marks the container unhealthy.
explain_choice: Restarting on exit is the restart policy's job; a health check catches the process that is still running but not working.
Ports are published with EXPOSE and -p, which say nothing about whether the service answers correctly.
The result shows in docker ps and inspect, but its purpose is to drive decisions, not to decorate the logs.

qs.q: How should a database password reach a production container?
a: Injected at run time, as a mounted secret or an environment variable
As a Dockerfile ARG, since build arguments are not kept in the image
Copied in as a .env file, then deleted again in a later build layer
Hardcoded in the code, but pushed to a private registry that few can pull
qs.e: Image layers are immutable archives that anyone who can pull the image can unpack, so a secret written into any layer stays readable even if a later layer deletes it. Supplying it at run time keeps it out of the image entirely; for secrets needed during a build, BuildKit's `RUN --mount=type=secret` avoids writing them into a layer.
explain_choice: ARG values used by a RUN step show up in docker history, so build arguments leak exactly what you tried to hide.
Deleting a file in a later layer only hides it; the earlier layer still contains it and can be extracted.
Private registries get shared, mirrored and leaked; access to the image should not mean access to the database.

qs.q: What is the main reason to run CI on every push, not just after merging?
a: To catch a failing test on the branch, before it can reach main
To deploy every commit, so production keeps matching the branch
To replace code review, since a green build means the code is right
So that developers no longer need to run any tests on their machines
qs.e: Feedback is cheapest while the change is small and its author still has it in their head. A required status check blocks the merge until tests, lint and type checks pass; a check that only runs after merge reports a problem everyone on main already has.
explain_choice: Continuous deployment is a separate decision; CI's job is to verify, and many teams deploy only tagged releases.
Tests check what someone thought to test; review catches design, naming and missing cases that no build can.
CI is the backstop, not the loop; running the fast tests locally still gives you answers in seconds instead of minutes.

qs.q: What does a rollback need in order to work under pressure?
a: The previous immutable image, plus migrations the old code can tolerate
A fresh database backup, restored just before you redeploy the old version
A rebuild from the old git tag, since it produces the same image
The :latest tag, pulled again on every host that runs the service
qs.e: Redeploying an artifact that already ran is fast and predictable. The usual blocker is the schema: if the new release dropped or renamed a column, the old code breaks against it. Expand-then-contract migrations (add first, remove only a release later) keep the previous version runnable.
explain_choice: Restoring a backup throws away every write since it was taken; it is disaster recovery, not a rollback.
A rebuild pulls whatever base image and dependency versions exist today, so it is a new, untested artifact.
:latest moves with every push, so it points at the release you are trying to get away from.

qs.q: An endpoint checks that you are logged in, but not that invoice 1043 is yours. Which OWASP risk is this?
a: Broken access control: an insecure direct object reference
Broken authentication, because the login check itself is too weak
Injection, because the invoice id is taken straight from the URL
Security misconfiguration of the web server's default settings
qs.e: Authentication establishes who you are; authorisation must then be checked on every request, for every object, on the server. One endpoint that forgets the ownership check exposes every record behind it, which is why broken access control is A01 in the OWASP Top 10 (2021).
explain_choice: The login works as intended; the flaw is what the logged-in user is allowed to reach afterwards.
The id is used as data, not code; nothing is injected, the server simply never asks who owns the record.
No setting is wrong; the missing ownership check is a design flaw in the application's own code.

qs.q: What actually defends against SQL injection?
a: Parameterised queries, so the values travel separately from the SQL text itself
Escaping every quote character in the input before building the string
Rejecting any input that contains SQL keywords such as DROP or UNION
Validating the length and type of each input at the API boundary
qs.e: With placeholders, the database parses the statement before the values are bound, so no value can change the query's structure. Escaping and keyword filters try to predict every dangerous input, and attackers get unlimited tries at the gap (numeric contexts, encodings, comments). Identifiers such as table names cannot be parameters, so allowlist those.
explain_choice: Escaping misses contexts where no quote is needed, such as `WHERE id = 1 OR 1=1`, and is easy to forget in one place.
Keyword blocklists break real input (a user called Union) and are bypassed with case, comments or encodings.
Validation narrows the input and is worth doing, but a valid-looking string can still carry SQL if it is concatenated.

qs.q: Your server fetches any URL a user supplies. What is the main risk?
a: SSRF: requests sent from inside your network to your internal services
XSS: the fetched page's scripts running in your other users' browsers
CSRF: the fetch riding on your users' own logged-in browser sessions
Mostly slow responses, which a strict timeout on every fetch will handle
qs.e: The request leaves from your server's network position, so it can reach what the attacker cannot: cloud metadata at 169.254.169.254, admin panels, databases on private addresses. Defend with an allowlist of destinations, resolve the host and check the IP before connecting (DNS rebinding), and do not follow redirects blindly.
explain_choice: XSS needs the fetched content rendered into a page for users; the fetch itself is dangerous even if nothing is shown.
CSRF abuses a victim's browser and cookies; here the server makes the request with its own network access.
A timeout limits how long a request can hang, not where it can go; an internal metadata call answers in milliseconds.

qs.q: What is rate limiting on a login endpoint mainly for?
a: Making brute force and credential stuffing too slow to be worth it
Cutting the CPU spent on slow password hashes during busy periods
Stopping a botnet that spreads its attempts over thousands of addresses
Protecting users from locking themselves out with wrong passwords
qs.e: Credential stuffing replays leaked username and password pairs, and brute force guesses; both need huge numbers of attempts, so throttling per account and per IP removes their economics. A distributed attack stays under per-IP limits, so pair throttling with MFA, breached-password checks and alerts on failure spikes.
explain_choice: It does save some hashing work, but that is a side effect; the goal is to deny attackers the volume of guesses they need.
A botnet spread over many addresses stays under per-IP limits, which is why throttling alone does not detect it.
Lockouts come from failed attempts, and rate limiting does nothing to prevent a user mistyping their own password.

qs.q: A dependency audit flags a known CVE in one of your packages. What is the right first step?
a: Check whether your code reaches the vulnerable path, then plan the upgrade
Nothing, as long as your own code does not import the affected module directly
Pin the current version, so that nothing changes under you while you look
Fork the library and patch the vulnerable function in your own copy
qs.e: Reachability decides urgency: a flaw in code you call with untrusted input needs a same-day fix or mitigation, one in an unused feature can ride the next release. Either way you upgrade, because the next change to your code may make it reachable. Tools such as pip-audit check transitive dependencies too.
explain_choice: Transitive dependencies run inside your process too; a library you import may call the vulnerable code for you.
Pinning freezes the vulnerable version in place; it stops accidental change but also stops the fix.
A private fork cuts you off from every later upstream security fix, which is usually worse than the original CVE.

qs.q: What should security logging capture?
a: Logins, access denials and admin actions, with no secrets or tokens
Full request bodies, so that any incident can be replayed exactly later
Errors alone, since successful requests are not security events
No user identifiers at all, so the logs hold nothing sensitive
qs.e: An investigation reconstructs who did what, when and from where, so the events that matter are authentication, authorisation failures and privileged changes, each tied to a user and a request id. Logs are copied widely and kept for a long time, so a logged password or token turns the log store into a breach of its own.
explain_choice: Request bodies contain passwords, tokens and personal data; logging them makes every log reader a potential attacker.
A successful login from a new country, or an admin granting rights, is often the breach; logging only errors misses it.
Without who did it, a log cannot answer the first question of any investigation; minimise data, do not remove identity.

qs.q: What is a prompt injection in an LLM-based system?
a: Untrusted text the model reads steering it into actions you did not intend
A user talking the model out of its safety training with a cleverly worded prompt
Malicious code slipped into the prompt template when the app is built
A chat-box problem, which goes away if users are not allowed free text
qs.e: The model cannot reliably tell instructions from data, so a web page, email or tool result it reads can carry commands that it then follows with your application's permissions. Treat all such content as untrusted input, and put real permission checks in front of any tool with side effects rather than relying on the prompt.
explain_choice: That is a jailbreak, aimed at the model's own rules; injection hijacks your application through content it processes.
Tampering with the template is a supply-chain problem; injection arrives at run time in content the model reads.
Indirect injection comes through retrieved documents, emails and tool output, with no attacker ever typing in the chat.

qs.q: What does defence in depth mean?
a: Several independent controls, so one failure is not a breach
One control made strong enough that it needs no backup behind it
Encrypting data at every layer, both at rest and in transit
Keeping the architecture secret, so attackers have nothing to plan with
qs.e: Every control eventually fails through a bug, a misconfiguration or a stolen credential, so the design question is what still stands when one does. Independence matters: controls that share a failure cause, such as one leaked admin key, count as one layer.
explain_choice: No single control survives every bug and misconfiguration; betting everything on one turns its first failure into a breach.
Encryption is one useful layer, but it does nothing against a request the application wrongly authorises.
Obscurity delays an attacker at best; once the design leaks, nothing is left, so it cannot be the strategy.

qs.q: Which systems may you run security tests against?
a: Only systems you own, or have written permission to test
Any public site, provided you report whatever you find
Any system at all, provided you cause no damage or downtime
Any site with a bug bounty, whatever its stated scope says
qs.e: Unauthorised access is a criminal offence in most jurisdictions (the Computer Misuse Act in the UK, the CFAA in the US) regardless of intent or harm. Written authorisation with a defined scope is what separates a security test from an attack.
explain_choice: Good intentions and a report afterwards do not create permission; the access itself is the offence.
Harm is not the test; merely accessing a system without authorisation is illegal in most places.
A bounty's scope is the permission; testing outside it is unauthorised, bounty or not.

QUIZZES.d: Models from scratch, and systems around them.

qs.q: What does backpropagation compute?
a: The gradient of the loss for every parameter, by the chain rule
The updated weights, by stepping each one against its gradient
The loss, by running the network from its output back to its input
Numerical gradients, by nudging each weight and re-running the net
qs.e: Reverse-mode automatic differentiation walks the computation graph from the loss back to the inputs, multiplying each node's local derivative by the gradient flowing in from above. One backward pass yields every parameter's gradient; a separate optimiser step (SGD, Adam) then decides how to change the weights.
